catalog:recovery:screen-curfew.evidenceSummary: A survey study separated the moment of going to bed from the later moment of attempting sleep, finding a measurable gap between the two driven mainly by electronic media use before bedtime. A separate systematic review of screen-limiting interventions in children found that reducing screen time before bed was linked with modestly longer and earlier sleep.

links.title: Bedtime, shuteye time and electronic media: sleep displacement is a two-step process
Interventions to control children's screen use and their effect on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis

protocols.population: 338 adults aged 18 to 25 completing an online survey, 67.6 percent women
protocols.regimen: Self-reported bedtime, shuteye time, and electronic media use before and after getting into bed
protocols.outcome: A thirty-nine-minute average gap between bedtime and shuteye time was found, driven almost entirely by pre-bedtime media use, and longer gaps were linked with poorer sleep ratings

source.title: Bedtime, shuteye time and electronic media: sleep displacement is a two-step process

protocols.population: 4,656 children aged 2 to 13 across eleven controlled intervention studies
protocols.regimen: Interventions that limited or restructured children's screen use before bedtime, compared with usual-care control groups
protocols.duration: Intervention periods reviewed ranged from under three months to longer programs, meta-analysis published 2020
protocols.outcome: Interventions that reduced screen use were linked with modest increases in sleep duration and earlier bedtimes compared with control groups

source.title: Interventions to control children's screen use and their effect on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis

benefits: Interventions that reduced children's screen use before bedtime were linked with modestly longer sleep duration and earlier bedtimes in the pooled trials.
Separating bedtime from the later moment of falling asleep let researchers isolate a thirty-nine-minute gap driven mainly by pre-bedtime media use.
Longer gaps between bedtime and sleep onset were linked with poorer self-rated sleep quality.
risks: The pooled screen-time trials showed only modest average effects, with sleep duration increasing by about eleven minutes a day.
It is not possible to determine from these studies whether reduced screen time directly improved sleep or reflected other changes made alongside it.
Most of the underlying evidence comes from self-report and observational designs rather than large randomized trials.
verdict.bottomLine: A systematic review of controlled interventions found reduced screen time before bed linked with modest gains in sleep duration and earlier bedtimes in children, while survey data in young adults linked pre-bedtime media use with a longer gap before falling asleep.

catalog:food-protocol:full-day-fast.evidenceSummary: A three-week randomised controlled trial in lean, healthy adults compared true 24-hour alternate-day fasting against a matched degree of continuous daily energy restriction, and against alternate-day fasting with no net energy deficit. True 24-hour fasting reduced body mass but lost less fat than the matched continuous restriction, and postprandial cardiometabolic markers and adipose tissue gene expression did not differ between groups.

links.title: A randomized controlled trial to isolate the effects of fasting and energy restriction on weight loss and metabolic health in lean adults (Templeman et al. 2021, Science Translational Medicine)

protocols.population: 36 lean, healthy adults split into three groups of 12
protocols.regimen: 24-hour fasting on alternate days, at either 150% or 200% energy intake on feeding days, compared with 75% energy intake every day with no fasting
protocols.outcome: Daily restriction cut fat mass by 1.75 kg; alternate-day fasting with the same net deficit cut it by only 0.74 kg, and fasting without a net deficit did not significantly reduce fat mass.

source.title: A randomized controlled trial to isolate the effects of fasting and energy restriction on weight loss and metabolic health in lean adults (Templeman et al. 2021, Science Translational Medicine)

benefits: A 24-hour fast repeated on alternate days lowered body mass in a 3-week randomised trial
risks: The same trial found this lost less fat than a matched degree of continuous daily restriction
Fasting without a net energy deficit did not significantly reduce body or fat mass
verdict.bottomLine: A single day of complete fasting cuts intake for that day; the trial evidence shows this loses less fat than the same calorie deficit spread evenly across days.
